prompt: An algorithm with an exact quadratic work model reaches its maximum input under a fixed time budget. Hardware becomes much faster while every operation gets the same speedup. Which statement explains the input-size gain?

options.text: Input capacity increases by the same factor as hardware speed
options.explanation: That is the linear-work pattern; quadratic work grows faster.

options.text: Input capacity cannot increase at all
options.explanation: More work can be done within the budget, so larger inputs become possible.

options.text: Input capacity increases by the square root of the speedup
options.explanation: Correct. The extra budget must cover the square of the input multiplier.

options.text: Every hardware doubling adds exactly one item
options.explanation: That describes constant-cost binary-choice enumeration, not quadratic work.

workedExample: Doubling a quadratic workload’s input needs roughly four times the work budget. Inverting that relationship gives a square-root input gain from a hardware speedup. The reasoning assumes uniform speed improvement and sufficient memory.

prompt: An exhaustive search checks every subset at constant cost. The computer becomes twice as fast, with the same time budget. What does this buy under the stated model?

options.explanation: Correct. Adding one binary choice doubles the number of subsets.
Doubling item count multiplies many binary choices; it does not merely double candidates.

options.text: A quadratic rather than exponential search
options.explanation: Hardware changes a constant factor, not the algorithm’s growth mechanism.

options.text: No additional input can be processed
options.explanation: The doubled work budget can cover one extra doubling of subset count.

workedExample: Each item is independently included or excluded. Adding one item doubles candidates, exactly using the doubled work budget. The conclusion depends on constant cost per subset check and does not define a universal practical input limit.
